groups.title: Moti del basso: diatonic, rising stepwise
groups.blurb: Bass motion only. The bass rises by step; the upper voices are set with a repeating interval pattern.

groups.title: Moti del basso: diatonic, descending stepwise
groups.blurb: The bass falls by step. These are the alternatives to the descending Rule of the Octave.

groups.title: Moti del basso: chromatic, rising
groups.blurb: Chromatic leading tones in the bass make each segment a small cadence in a new key.

groups.title: Moti del basso: chromatic, descending (laments)
groups.blurb: The chromatic tetrachord ①–⑤ in the bass: Lamento and Morte.

groups.title: Moti del basso: disjunct (sequences)
groups.blurb: Sequential basses. A model (prototype) is transposed by a second up or down; the Romanesca is the exception (down a third). Swapping the metric position of bass and chords ("metric inversion") creates a different pattern: A→B ≠ B→A.

groups.title: Schemata: Romanesca, Prinner and opening gambits
groups.blurb: Schemata = a bass motion plus a set of upper voices. Embellishment by suspensions, non-chord tones, bass motion and combinations.

groups.title: Schemata: changing-note (dichotomous) schemata
groups.blurb: Double-neighbour melodic shapes split into a question (opening) and an answer (closing). Aprile, Meyer and paired Do-Re-Mi can sound simultaneously.

groups.title: Schemata: Folia, Fonte, Monte, Monte Romanesca
groups.blurb: Larger sequential schemata, typically opening the second half of a binary form.

groups.title: Schemata on pedal points: Quiescenza, Ponte, Indugio, Fenaroli
groups.blurb: Pedal points on ①, ⑤ or ④ with stereotyped chord successions.

groups.title: Combinations of schemata
groups.blurb: Schemata chained into phrases; harmonic rhythm often accelerates.

patterns.name: 5–6 (stepwise Monte)
patterns.summary: Each bass note carries a 5/3 then a 6/3. The sixth is tied over and becomes the fifth of the next bar, so the potential parallel fifths are broken up.
rules: The 6 on each bass note is held into the next bar as its 5 (tie).
In 3 parts, one upper voice moves in parallel thirds (tenths) with the bass; the other does the 5–6.
guidelines: Major: can span the whole octave.
Minor: usually breaks off after ④ and closes ⑤ (5–7) → ①.
Invertible: 6↔3 and 4↔5 (green marks in notes p.1).

examples.title: Minor, 3 parts, closing ⑤ 5–7 → ①
examples.caption: Melodic-minor inflections (F♯, G♯) follow the rising bass, as in the notes.

sources.fenaroli: Book III, “Moves of the partimento”: rising stepwise I (5th moving to 6th)

checks: HCP: “The Monte is a stepwise ascending sequence, in which 5/3 and 6/3 chords alternate.”
Demeyere: sixth tied to the next fifth; major spans an octave, minor stops after ④ while the bass still rises to ⑤.
Fenaroli III: rising stepwise, rule I = 5th moving to 6th, 6th held as next 5th.

patterns.name: 3–6 progression (3–6 Monte)
patterns.summary: Two-part origin of the Monte: the upper voice alternates a third and a sixth over each bass note, leaping a fourth up and a third down.
rules: Upper voice: 3 → 6 over the same bass note (4th up), then 3 over the next bass note (3rd down).
guidelines: The second type of 3–6 progression is the schema Third Down Second Up (see disjunct moti).
Minor: raise ⑥ and ⑦ when the bass ascends (melodic minor).

variants.name: 3-part 3–6 Monte
variants.description: Three-part setting adding a voice to the 3–6 alternation (5/3 → 6/3 per bass note).
variants.review: The voice assignment of the 3-part version on notes p.1 is ambiguous; no realization generated.

sources.notes: Moti del Basso p.1; HCP Notes p.1 (§1.2)

checks: HCP Terms: “two types of 3–6 progressions … alternation of thirds and sixths on a stepwise bass … second type is Third Down Second Up.”
flags: 3-part voicing not realized (ambiguous in the notes).

patterns.summary: The octave of each bass note is held as a 7th over the next one, resolves to 6, then leaps up a third to the new octave.
rules: 7 must be prepared (tied) and resolve down by step to 6.
Each resolution is followed by a rising third (back to the octave).
guidelines: Major can span the octave; minor only a fourth.
Minor alternative from ④: 7–6 5 | 9–8 7 | 3/8 (notes p.1).

sources.fenaroli: Book III, rising stepwise II (7th resolving to 6th)

checks: Demeyere: “each resolution must be followed by a rising third”; major spans an octave, minor a fourth.
Fenaroli III rule II: octave held as 7th, resolves to 6th, rises a 3rd to the octave.

patterns.summary: The tenth of each bass note is held as a 9th over the next, resolves to 8, then leaps to the new tenth. An optional 5–6 in the other voice (□ in the notes) smooths the chord change.
rules: 9 prepared by 10, resolves to 8.
Stop at ⑤: continuing to ⑥–⑦ would double the leading tone (crossed out in notes p.1).
guidelines: Cadence: ⑤ 9–8 7 → ① 3/8.
Minor: add a passing ⑦ (G in A minor) in the middle voice to avoid the augmented second.

examples.title: Major, 3 parts
examples.caption: The second half of each bar shows the optional 5–6 shift in the middle voice.

checks: Demeyere: “The 9–8 pattern breaks off at ⑤, probably to avoid doubling the leading note there”; minor needs an added g¹ to avoid the augmented second.

patterns.name: (10–)9–8 with leapfrog (Corellian)
patterns.summary: The two upper voices take turns: one resolves 9–8 and then leaps a fourth up to the third of the next bass note, while the other is suspended.
rules: Each octave resolution leaps a 4th up to the 3rd over the next bass note.
Avoid the melodic tritone in the middle voice.
guidelines: The voices cross every bar (that is the “leapfrog”).
Also used under the Folia (notes p.26) and the minor Stabat-Mater-type basses.

checks: Demeyere: “Each octave resolution leaps a fourth to the third on the next bass note, and the middle voice avoids the melodic tritone.”

patterns.name: (10/8–)9/7–8/6 combined
patterns.summary: The 9–8 and 7–6 chains run simultaneously in the two upper voices, giving a richer harmony.
rules: Both suspensions prepared together (10 and 8) and resolved together (8 and 6).

checks: Demeyere: “(10/8–)9/7–8/6: Both suspension chains run simultaneously.”

patterns.name: Stepwise Romanesca (moto)
aka: alternative for the descending Rule of the Octave
patterns.bass: ①–⑦–⑥–⑤–④–③ (+ ②–① to complete the octave)
patterns.summary: Bass notes alternate 5/3 (strong) and 6/3 (weak). Soprano either in parallel thirds with the bass, or leaping (3rd up, 5th down).
rules: One sonority per bass note: 5/3 on strong, 6/3 on weak beats.
To span the octave append ②–① with 6/3 → 5/3.
Minor: use the natural ⑥ and ⑦ (natural minor).
guidelines: Voices available: 5–6, 3–3 (parallel thirds), 3–6 (leaping).
Inverts with the leaping Romanesca (see Schemata).

checks: HCP Terms: stepwise Romanesca usually ①→③; 5/3 on strong, 6/3 on weak beats.
Demeyere: alternative for the descending RO; append ②–① to span an octave; melody stepwise (parallel thirds) or leaping.

patterns.name: 7–6 Fauxbourdon
patterns.summary: One upper voice in parallel thirds (tenths) with the bass; the other forms a chain of 7–6 suspensions. Each 6 is the preparation of the next 7.
rules: Each 7 tied from the previous 6 and resolved to 6.
Ends with the compound cadence 7–6(♯) → 8 over ②–①.
guidelines: Embellished fauxbourdon; mirrors the 5–6 Monte in descent (HCP).
Can span a full octave in both modes.

sources.notes: Moti del Basso p.2; HCP Notes p.4

checks: HCP Terms: “The 7–6 Fauxbourdon mirrors the Monte in a descending motion, with 7/3 and 6/3 chords alternating.”

patterns.name: Fauxbourdon (parallel 6/3)
patterns.summary: Chains of 6/3 chords between 5/3 anchors. In your notes this is marked “move to R.O.” (it is the default realization of the stepwise RO without anchors).
rules: Not invertible: exchanging the two upper voices turns their parallel fourths into parallel fifths.
Parallel 5/3 chords must be avoided (parallel fifths/octaves).
guidelines: Begin and end with (5)/3 on ①.
Minor: raised ⑥ and ⑦ ascending, natural descending.

sources.notes: Moti del Basso p.1 (crossed: “move to R.O.”); HCP Notes p.3

checks: HCP Terms: “Fauxbourdon is … the parallel progression of 6/3 chords”; parallel 5/3 chords must be avoided.

patterns.name: 5–6/4+/2–6 (elaborated stepwise Romanesca)
patterns.summary: Each odd bass note takes 5/3 then 6/4+/2; each even bass note takes 6/3. Every pair is a local ④–③ (in V, iii/III and I).
rules: The 4+ resolves up to the 6 of the next bass note; the bass resolves down by step.
guidelines: Usually major.
Your notes ask: “inverted fonte-romanesca?” — Demeyere confirms Byros’s label.

checks: Demeyere: “Each uneven bass note takes a triad, then a 6/4+/2 chord; each even bass note takes one sixth chord … local ④–③ … typically major … Byros labels it an inverted Fonte-Romanesca.”

patterns.name: Chromatic 5–6 (descending)
patterns.summary: Most bass notes take 5/3 then 6/3 with chromatic inflections, tonicizing VI, (V), IV, (III), II on the way down. The upper voices combine a descending chromatic line and an ascending diatonic one.
rules: Each 6 resolves (→8) as a local leading-tone motion into the next key.
guidelines: Contains the Fonte-Romanesca in its first segment.
Several distributions exist (notes p.3 shows two major and three minor versions).

checks: Demeyere: derived from settings by Muscogiuri and Lavigna (not Fenaroli’s regole); Fonte-Romanesca appears in the first excerpt.
flags: Dense chromatic voice distribution: no automatic realization generated; transcribe directly from notes p.3 when building.

patterns.name: Tied bass: (5–)6/4+/2–6(/5)
patterns.bass: ① ⑧ ⌒ ⑦ ⌒ ⑥ ⌒ ⑤ ⌒ ④ ⌒ ③ (syncopated)
patterns.summary: The bass is syncopated: each tied bass note is a 2nd (4/2) against the upper voices on the strong beat and resolves down to a 6/3 on the weak beat.
rules: Each tied bass note is a suspension: prepared, sounded against 4/2 (or 6/4/2) on the strong beat, resolved down by step.
At the syncopated ④ the 4 must be augmented (6/4+/2) — “④ MUST w/ 4+”.
The pattern stops on ③; then a cadence (e.g., ② 6/5 – ⑤ – ①).
guidelines: Variant I: 6/4+/2 on every strong beat (scale mutations; local ④→③ in V, IV, iii, I…).
Variant II: diatonic 6/4/2 strong, 6/3 weak.
Variant III: 6/4/2 strong, 6/5/3 weak.
3 parts: drop the 6–8 line → 4/2 – 6/3 (HCP §2.5).
2 parts: 2–6 over the tied bass (HCP §1.4).
Opening gambit: ① ⑧⌒ ⑦♯ → ① with 2–3 / 4–6 figures (notes p.4).

examples.title: Variant II, 4 parts, major
examples.caption: At ④ the 4 is the augmented fourth (diatonic in major). Ends with the compound cadence ② 6/5 → ⑤ 7 → ①.

sources.notes: Moti del Basso p.4; HCP Notes p.5
sources.fenaroli: Book III “Partimento that descends in ties”

checks: Demeyere: three settings (6/4+/2 + 6; diatonic 6/4/2 + 6; 6/4/2 + 6/5); syncopated ④ requires 6/4+/2; 3-part omits the sixth → 4(+)/2.
HCP Terms: 4/2 on the tied (strong) beat, 6/3 on the weak beat; 3-part variant of the two-part 2–3 schema.
Fenaroli III: descending in ties — the last tied 4th “should definitely be augmented”; don’t descend this way beyond ④.

patterns.name: Chromatic Monte (③→⑥)
patterns.summary: Each segment is a local ⑦–① cadence: 6/3 (or 6/5) on the chromatic leading tone, 5/3 on the new local tonic. Tonicizes IV, V, vi.
rules: The chromatic leading tones sit in the bass and rise to the local tonic.
Avoid doubling the leading tone in 4 parts (the struck 8 in notes p.5).
guidelines: Embellish with 4–3 suspensions, or invertible 4–3/9–8 pairs.
Two-segment version ends on ⑤ and also occurs in minor.
Major ③→⑥ equals ⑤→① in the relative minor.

variants.name: Minor ⑤→①
variants.description: Bass ⑤–⑥–♯⑥–⑦–♯⑦–①; tonicizes VI, VII, i. Can be embellished by 9–8/7–6 or 4–3/9–8 suspensions.
variants.review: Not auto-realized; transcribe from notes p.5.

checks: HCP Terms: chromaticism best in the bass; leading tones support secondary dominants (6/3 or 6/5); usual tonicizations ii, IV, V, vi.
Demeyere: ③, ♯④, ♯⑤ act as local leading notes; Fenaroli links it to major and ends on ⑥.

patterns.name: Lamento: (6–)7–6
patterns.summary: Chromatic descent ①→⑤ realized with 7–6 suspensions over each pair of bass notes; ends with ⑥–⑤ as an augmented sixth or a Phrygian half cadence.
rules: Best in 3 parts.
In 4 parts the fourth voice (mostly the tenor) is forced to leap to avoid parallel octaves.
guidelines: ⑥–⑤: augmented sixth (♯④ over ♭⑥, per the RO) or major sixth (Phrygian cadence).
Represents lament / suffering; common as a Baroque basso ostinato.

examples.title: 3 parts, A minor, ending with the augmented sixth

variants.name: Lamento 6–6 (simplified)
variants.description: Only sixth chords; normally three voices in one position (exchanging the upper voices creates fifths).

checks: HCP Terms: Lamento fits best in 3 parts; in 4 parts the fourth voice (mostly tenor) must leap to prevent parallel octaves.
Demeyere: chain of 7–6; ⑥–⑤ with augmented sixth or Phrygian cadence; 6–6 version in one position only.

patterns.name: Morte
patterns.summary: Same chromatic bass as the Lamento, different harmony: the upper voice moves in contrary motion; ⑦♭ carries an active 6/4+/2 (④→③ in the IV key); ♭⑥ an augmented sixth.
rules: The 6/4+/2 on the lowered ⑦ resolves to 6/3 on ⑥ (tonicizes IV).
guidelines: Can open a piece (contrary motion between ① and ⑤).
Alternative segment 3 uses a passing 6/4 to avoid parallel fifths.

checks: HCP Terms: Morte shares the Lamento bass; both modes; upper voice in contrary motion; lowered ⑦ supports a secondary 4/2 → 6/3 on ⑥ (IV).
Demeyere: 6/+4/2 on ♭⑦; common in major.

patterns.name: Second up, third down
patterns.summary: Strong beats: 6 or 6/5; weak beats: 5/3.
rules: Bad for opening a piece: it starts on a 6/3 or 6/5 chord.
guidelines: 5/3 on the weak beat sounds unstable → prefer the metric complement, third down second up.
Rare in partimenti because its meter is unclear.

checks: Demeyere: strong beats 6 or 6/5, weak beats triad; not suitable for opening; rare, tends to sound like Third Down Second Up.

patterns.name: Third down, second up
patterns.summary: Strong beats: 5/3; weak beats: 6 or 6/5. Derived from the two-part 3–6 progression.
rules: Fits the meter (5/3 on the strong beat).
guidelines: Embellish with 10–9–3 suspensions (4 parts) or with (5–)7–6 and (3–)9–8 together (“2 perspectives”).

checks: HCP Terms: Third Down Second Up alternates 6/5 and 5/3 (6/3 may replace 6/5).
Demeyere: usually ①→⑤ or ④→①; triad on strong beats.

patterns.name: Third up, second down
patterns.bass: ①–③ | ②–④ | ③–⑤ | ④–⑥ | ⑤ → ①
patterns.summary: The first bass note of each segment takes a 7–6 suspension, the second a sixth chord.
rules: The first-bass-note suspensions are the defining feature (7–6, or 3–4–3 in the 4-part version).
guidelines: Better in triple time.
4 parts: each falling second becomes a local ②→① clausula tenorizans with a 3–4–3 suspension.

checks: Demeyere version 1: 7–6 on each first bass note, sixth chord on the second; version 2: local ②–① clausula tenorizans with 4–3.

patterns.name: Fourth down, second up (leaping Romanesca / Pachelbel bass)
patterns.summary: Upper voices in parallel thirds; complete and incomplete 5/3 alternate. The only sequence whose model is transposed down a third.
rules: Minor: natural ⑥ and ⑦.
guidelines: (8–)4–3 / (3–)9–8 suspensions are invertible — keep them for 3 parts.
Full schema material (embellishments, stretto, endings) is under Schemata → Leaping Romanesca.

checks: HCP §5.1: leaping Romanesca, 4–3/9–8 alternation; only complete 5/3 chords require 4 parts.

patterns.name: Fourth up, third down (Monte Principale)
patterns.summary: Each segment’s first chord can take a major third, making each segment a local ⑤→① (tonicizing V and vi). Not the same as the stepwise Monte.
rules: Usually major.
guidelines: Embellish with (5–)9–8 (voice crossing) and/or (7–)4–3 to avoid leading tone → tonic doubling.
Gjerdingen added “principale” to distinguish it from the stepwise Monte.

sources.fenaroli: Book III “Partimento that rises by fourth and descends by third”

checks: HCP Terms: leaping chromatic variant with rising fourths = Monte Principale.
Fenaroli III: rises 4th / falls 3rd — 9th prepared by the 5th on the note a 4th up.

patterns.name: Fourth up, fifth down (descending circle of fifths, Quintfall)
patterns.summary: Triads only in the basic version; a 7–3 suspension chain (both upper voices alternately) or 9–8 / 9–5 suspensions enrich it. Fifth down fourth up is the same with the octaves of every second bass note swapped.
rules: Melodic tritones (④–⑦ major, ♭⑥–② minor) are accepted inside the sequence.
Strong beat on ① (or on ④ with ① as upbeat).
guidelines: Minor: ④–♭⑦–♭③ forms a local ②–⑤–① in the relative major.
The 7–3 chain is invertible.

variants.name: Chain of dominants (chromatic 5↓4↑)
variants.description: Every chord becomes a (secondary) dominant of the next: major triads and/or dominant sevenths; the third descends chromatically while the seventh resolves.

sources.fenaroli: Book III “Partimento that rises a fourth” / “falls a fourth”

checks: Demeyere: basic version triads only; seventh chain in 3 parts; ninths on ④, (♭)③, ②; melodic tritones accepted.
HCP Terms: Chain of Dominants is the chromatic variant of Fifth Down Fourth Up; the leading tone descends by a chromatic half tone.
Compendium: “Quintfall” sequence (7th run) and its inversions.

patterns.name: Fifth up, fourth down (Monte Romanesca, Quartfall)
patterns.summary: Model like the Romanesca but the second bass note an octave higher; triads only in teaching, canonic 4–3 version in real compositions.
rules: Major only.
Third segment (optional) becomes a local ①–⑤ to avoid the diminished fifth on ⑦.
guidelines: Canonic Monte Romanesca: (8–)4–3 suspensions alternate between the upper voices (proposta/risposta).

sources.fenaroli: Book III “Partimento that rises a fifth” (4th prepared by the 8ve)

checks: Demeyere: major only; third segment a local ①–⑤; canonic 4–3 variant used in compositions.
Fenaroli III rises a fifth II: 4th prepared by the 8ve resolved to the 3rd.

patterns.name: Sixth up, fifth down (= third down, fourth up)
patterns.summary: Alternating 5/3 and 6/3: each bass pair is a local ⑤–③, so the pattern is a Monte with exchanged outer voices.
guidelines: Remove the octaves for 3 parts.
Add a (5–)7–6 suspension on the second note of each segment.
Fenaroli: this motion is equivalent to one that descends a third and rises a fourth.

sources.fenaroli: Book III “Partimento that rises a sixth”

checks: Demeyere: version (b) alternates triads and sixth chords — local ⑤–③, a Monte with exchanged outer voices; 7–6 on the second note.
Fenaroli III: “this motion is equivalent to one that descends a 3rd and rises a 4th.”

patterns.name: Leaping Romanesca
patterns.summary: Opening schema; Pachelbel’s Canon is “the” exemplar. Upper voices in parallel thirds; complete and incomplete 5/3 alternate.
rules: Minor uses the natural scale (⑥♮, ⑦♮).
Only complete 5/3 chords → 4 parts required.
guidelines: Suspensions: (5–)4–3 in 2 parts; (8–)4–3 / (3–)9–8 in 3 parts (invertible); add (5–)4–3 for a third chain.

Embellish the embellishments: repeated notes; escape tone (step then leap); repeated notes + escape tone; upper neighbour; double neighbour; lower neighbour + escape tone; arpeggiation (compound line: two voices merged into one); lower neighbour + arpeggio; passing tones; passing tones + arpeggio; rests (offbeat entries); combinations of the above.
If the bass is embellished (chordal skips, Insanguine, Durante or Fenaroli running basses), keep the upper voices plain.
3-part embellishment: one upper voice; or two voices in parallel/complementary (canonic) motion; bariolage as a keyboard technique.
With 6/4+ (Fenaroli): the bass may fall a perfect 4th with 6/4+; with 6/4+/2 the bass must step down.

variants.name: Temporary key change
variants.description: 2 parts: turn a rising second into a discant cadence (⑤♯→⑥, ③♯→④) or a deceptive cadence (⑤→⑥) → leads to the Fonte-Romanesca (I, vi, IV keys). Applies to 3 parts too.

variants.name: Stretto
variants.description: 2 parts: second voice enters a bar late at the 3rd (stretto sine pausa = without the rest). Stretto per arsin et thesin uses syncopations (9–3). 3 parts: avoid parallel fifths by doubling the 3rd at the end.

variants.name: Modified and shortened end
variants.description: Only two segments, then a cadence: in major the ④ gets 6/3 instead of 5/3 and continues as a Galant cadence (⑤→①) or a Prinner (③–②–①); in minor ③ takes 6/3 → ④ – ⑤ – ① G.C.

checks: HCP §5.1 Terms: Pachelbel exemplar; inverts with stepwise Romanesca; 4–3 and 9–8 suspensions; natural minor.
Demeyere: section titles match the note structure (embellishment parts 1–2, three-part, stretto, modified/shortened end).

patterns.name: Stepwise Romanesca
patterns.summary: Stepwise diatonic descent; it is the leaping Romanesca in invertible counterpoint. Often extended by a Prinner (④–③–②–①).
rules: Avoid the incomplete 6/3 with doubled 6th (3↑6 over 8↓6).
Minor: use ⑥♮ and ⑦♮ (natural minor) — less common.
guidelines: 3-part options: 3/8 | 3/6; or 3/5 (invertible); or 3↑6 with 3↓2 voices.
(3–)2–3 suspensions in either voice, or as a syncopated/tied bass.
Temporary key change: ⑦ → ⑥ as 4+ (vi key), ⑤ → ④ (IV key).
Embellishments: same choices as the leaping Romanesca.

checks: HCP: stepwise ↔ leaping Romanesca by invertible counterpoint; suspensions less frequent but possible; natural minor.

patterns.name: Prinner
patterns.summary: The galant riposte: answers an opening gambit. In 3 parts a third voice is nearly stationary on ① (upper voice in the 17th c., middle in the 18th c.).
rules: 5/3 on ④ (deviates from the descending RO).
Modulating Prinner (①–⑦–⑥–⑤ = ④–③–②–① of V) needs ⑥ raised; it does not exist in minor.
guidelines: Best in major (graceful).
With 7–6 on ②: stage 3 twice as long as stage 1.
High ② drop: conventional ornamental sign of impending closure.
Incomplete Prinner: repeat stages 1–2 (④–③, ④–③, ④–③–②–①).

variants.name: Bass ④–③–②–⑤–①
variants.description: Turns the Prinner into an authentic cadence; 7–6 then 7 → 3♯ → 8. Can start on the upbeat.

variants.name: Bass ④–③–②–⑦–①
variants.description: Sixth chord on ⑦ to avoid voice-leading problems.

variants.name: Other bass lines
variants.description: ④–③–⑦–①; ③–④–⑤–① (⑤ as passing tone); ④–①–⑤–① (IAC); ④–①–⑤–⑥ (deceptive); ④–①–⑦–①; ①–①–⑦–① (Mozart K.545/i bars 1–4); ①–①–②–⑦–①; ①–①–②–⑤–①; ①–①–⑤–①.

variants.name: Expanded Prinner
variants.description: Bass ④–① | ③–⑥ | ②–⑤ | ① with 7–3 suspensions.
variants.figures: 5 3 | 7 3 | 7 3♯→8 over ④ ① | ③ ⑥ | ② ⑤ | ①

variants.name: Canonic Prinner
variants.description: Upper voice and bass in canon (proposta/risposta): bass ⑥–⑤ | ④–③ | ②–①.

sources.notes: Moti del Basso pp.17–18; HCP Notes p.11

checks: HCP Terms: 5/3 on ④ deviates from the descending RO; modulating Prinner needs raised sixth on ⑥ and doesn’t exist in minor; best in major.
Demeyere: riposte; mild ②–① clausula tenorizans; stage 3 with 7–6 often twice as long; High ② drop “a conventional sign of impending closure” (Gjerdingen 2007, p.74).

patterns.name: Stabat Mater Prinner (SMP)
patterns.melody: top ⑥–⑤–④–③; middle (⑤)–④–③–②–① metrically shifted (2–3 suspensions)
patterns.summary: Dominant pedal (≈ Quiescenza on ⑤) + a Prinner top line + a metrically shifted descent in the middle voice that produces a chain of 2–3 suspensions. Named after the “Amen” of Pergolesi’s Stabat Mater.
rules: In 3 voices the chordal 7th and the leading tone cannot be doubled (half-cadence version: use ④♯ in minor).
guidelines: Optional 4th voice: ②↑ ③↓ on the dominant pedal (⑦ ① ② ⑦ ① ⑥ ⑦ ①; ①♯ optional in major).
Mozart loves the IAC/broken-cadence type.

checks: Demeyere: dominant pedal; top ➏–➎–➍–➌; metrically shifted ➎–➍–➌–➋–➊ with 2–3 suspensions; functions IAC/PAC/broken, half cadence; Pergolesi Amen bars 45–51a.
flags: Demeyere calls the bass motion “Second Up Third Down” — in your notes that line is the optional tenor over the pedal. Both readings describe the same texture.
Not auto-realized: voice layout over the pedal is dense; transcribe from notes p.19.

patterns.name: Do-Re-Mi
patterns.summary: Proposta schema that opens a piece or section. Melody and bass are invertible (Do-Re-Mi can also sit in the bass under ①–⑦–①).
rules: 3 parts over ①–⑦–①: ④→③ in the middle would double the third on ① — hold ⑤ instead.
guidelines: 18th-c. embellishment: “Adeste Fideles leaps” (broken chord).
With suspension: 8⌒9–3 over ① ⑦ ① (4/2, 5/2 or 6/4/2 sonorities); 5/2 sounds empty in 4 parts.
Bass ①–②–③ with melody ①–⑦–① (add parallel thirds for 3 voices).

examples.title: Do-Re-Mi in the bass, melody ①–⑦–①

checks: Demeyere: proposta, ➊–➋–➌ over ①–⑦–①; Do-Sol-Do; suspension → 4/2 or 5/2 (3 parts), 5/2, 5/4/2, 6/4/2 (4 parts); Do-Fa&Sol-Do; Do-Re-Mi in the bass.

patterns.name: Paired Do-Re-Mi
patterns.summary: An extra Re splits the Do-Re-Mi into a question (opens) and an answer (closes).
guidelines: Chromatic version (most popular): chromatic appoggiaturas / passing notes ①♯ and ②♯ (9♯→3, 4♯→5).

checks: Demeyere: Gjerdingen’s label; question/answer pairs; ①–⑦…⑦–① and ①–⑤…⑤–① basses; chromatic form most popular.

patterns.name: Sol-Fa-Mi
patterns.summary: Proposta schema: the melody descends ⑤–④, then repeats ④–③ over a closing bass.
guidelines: ② can take a 6/3 chord, or 7/5/3 on ⑤ in the ⑤–① version.

sources.other: Gjerdingen, Music in the Galant Style (2007), Sol-Fa-Mi

flags: No Sol-Fa-Mi page on essaysonmusic.com and not in HCP; check against Gjerdingen ch. “The Sol-Fa-Mi” if available.

patterns.name: Meyer
patterns.summary: Changing-note schemata: double-neighbour shapes (↗↘↗ or ↘↗↘) forming a question (harmonically & melodically opening) and an answer (closing). The Meyer melody ①–⑦…④–③.
guidelines: ①–②…⑦–①: clausula cantizans → weaker close; ①–②…⑤–①: clausula basizans → stronger.
Stage 2 can be metrically doubled so stage 3 falls on a weak beat.
Typical cantizans gesture ⑥–⑤–④–③ in the second dyad.
Suspensions often on stages 2 and 4 (e.g., 8⌒7→6♯, 5⌒7–6 8 4–3).

variants.name: Other basses
variants.description: ①–⑤…⑤–①; ①–⑤…⑦–①.

checks: Demeyere: treble ➊–➐…➍–➌; basses ①–②…⑦–①, metrically shifted, ①–②…⑤–① (somewhat stronger), ①–⑤…⑤–①, ①–⑤…⑦–①, ①–②…⑤–⑥.

patterns.name: Aprile
patterns.summary: Changing-note schemata: double-neighbour shapes (↗↘↗ or ↘↗↘) forming a question (harmonically & melodically opening) and an answer (closing). Shares its first dyad with the Meyer; the answer is ②–①.
guidelines: Optional suspensions on stages 2 and/or 4 (7/4/3 and 9/4).
①–②…④–③ bass = the Jupiter bass (clausula altizans).

variants.name: Other basses
variants.description: ①–②…④–③ (Jupiter); ①–⑤…⑤–①; ①–⑤…⑦–①; ③–④…④–③ (6/3 4+/2 | 6/2 6/3).

checks: Demeyere: treble ➊–➐…➋–➊; same set of basses including ③–④…④–③ and the Jupiter bass.

patterns.name: Pastorella
patterns.bass: ①–⑤ … ⑤–① (or …⑦–①, or pedal on ①)
patterns.summary: Changing-note schemata: double-neighbour shapes (↗↘↗ or ↘↗↘) forming a question (harmonically & melodically opening) and an answer (closing). Melody ③–②…④–③; in parallel thirds below it gives the Aprile treble.
guidelines: Optional suspensions on stages 2 and/or 4.
Pedal-point version on ① with 7/4/2 on stages 2–3.

checks: Demeyere: ➌–➋…➍–➌; basses ①–⑤…⑤–①, ①–⑤…⑦–①, pedal on ① (7/4/2).

patterns.name: Jupiter
patterns.summary: Changing-note schemata: double-neighbour shapes (↗↘↗ or ↘↗↘) forming a question (harmonically & melodically opening) and an answer (closing). Melody ①–②…④–③ (Mozart K.551 finale). With ④ in stage 2 the dichotomy disappears (single gesture).
guidelines: Optional suspensions on stages 2 and/or 4.
③–④–⑤–⑥ bass ends deceptively.

variants.name: Other basses
variants.description: ③–④–⑤–① ; ③–④–⑤–⑥ (deceptive).

checks: Demeyere: ①–⑤…⑤–① dichotomous; ①–④–⑤–① single gesture; ③–④–⑤–① and ③–④–⑤–⑥ variants.
flags: The web page is inconsistent about the first melody note (➊ vs ➌); your notes and Gjerdingen give ①–②…④–③.

patterns.name: Folia
patterns.summary: Late Folia (17th–18th c.), usually in D minor, in 3/4 with the sarabande rhythm. Bass moves by fourths and seconds; temporary turn to the relative major (♭⑦–♭③).
rules: Minor only (Dorian colour: no ⑥ in the bass, ⑦♮).
First phrase ends with a half cadence; second with a clausula basizans.
guidelines: Rhythm: odd bars ♩ ♩. ♪ (sarabande), even bars shorter values with inégalité.
Alternative treble a third above / sixth below; combine both for 3 parts (compound line).
Corelli leapfrog setting; extra harmonies (⑦♯ passing tone, ⑥♯ toward the relative major, chromatic passing tones).
Bars 4–5 can be read as a sequential transposition of bars 2–3 (4↑2↓); bars 5–8 as a leaping Romanesca (4↓2↑).

examples.title: Standard + alternative treble, 3 parts
examples.caption: Framework only (one sonority per bar); add the sarabande rhythm in the melody.

sources.notes: Moti del Basso pp.25–26; HCP Notes p.12

checks: HCP Terms: parallel sixths or thirds; complete/incomplete 5/3; minor only.
Demeyere: bass ①–⑤–①–♭⑦–♭③–♭⑦; standard treble 1–7–1–2–♭3–2–1–7; alternative treble; Corelli leapfrog (hypothetical); extra harmonies (C.P.E. Bach, Corelli).

patterns.name: Fonte
patterns.bass: ①♯–② | ⑦–① (each segment a ⑦→① cadence)
function: opens the 2nd half of a (rounded) binary form
patterns.summary: Two-segment descending sequence: segment 1 in the ii key, segment 2 in I, each a clausula cantizans with a ④–③ melody. Named by Riepel (1755).
rules: Major only (ii° in minor cannot form a triad). In a minor piece use the relative major (“borrowed Fonte”).
guidelines: Melody ⑥–⑤–④–③ (V6 → V6/5 → i, V6 → V6/5 → I).
Jommelli: ⑥(♭) on ⑦ in each segment (vii°7); the literally transposed ⑥♭ is the “hermaphrodite tone” (Riepel disliked it, Mozart used it).
Suspensions 4–3 and/or 9–8 on the second chord.
Bass ⑤–①; bass ⑦–⑤–① (temporary 3/2 in 4/4).
Chromatic Fonte: Picardy third in the II key.
Metrically shifted Fonte possible.

variants.name: Extended Fonte
variants.description: Each segment holds two different cadences (cantizans + basizans, or altizans + cantizans), or a whole phrase with several cadential gestures.

variants.name: Triple Fonte
variants.description: Three segments: iii key → ii key → I key.

variants.name: Fonte in other keys
variants.description: Finishing in V (vi → V; D. Cimarosa); starting in v and finishing in IV (rare).

checks: HCP Terms: escapes and returns; after the medial repeat sign; ①♯–② with 6–5–4 then ⑦–① with 5–4–3; major only, relative major in minor pieces; dim7 may replace V7.
Demeyere: Riepel (1755/57); Jommelli; hermaphrodite note; ⑤–① and ⑦–⑤–① basses; chromatic and metrically shifted Fonte.

patterns.name: Monte
patterns.melody: each segment a cadence (often ⑦→① clausula cantizans)
function: opens the 2nd half of a binary form (alternative to the Fonte)
patterns.summary: Ascending sequence of cadences starting in the subdominant key; “mountain”.
rules: A key is defined by A4→6 or d5→3.
guidelines: 2 segments: IV–V. 3: IV–V–vi, or IV(iv)–V–I(i). 4: IV–V–vi–I. 5: IV–V–vi–I–I (vii° sounds too dissonant, so segment 4 stays in I).
Minor Monte ending in v: use V instead of v (the second segment is key-ambiguous).
Rare: major Monte ending in v; (♭VI–)♭vii–i Monte.
IV–I Monte: clausula altizans.
Borrowed Monte: in a minor piece, take the Monte from the relative major.

checks: Demeyere: IV then V; IV–V–vi; IV–V–I/iv–V–i; IV–V–vi–I; IV–V–vi–I–I; minor Monte possible.
flags: The A4→6 / d5→3 key-definition rule is from your notes (Demeyere does not phrase it that way).

patterns.name: Monte Romanesca
patterns.bass: leaping: ①–⑤ | ②–⑥ | (③–⑦); stepwise: ①–⑦♭ | ②–① | ③
patterns.summary: A schema of its own (not Monte, not Romanesca): 2, 2½ or 3 segments; leaping (5↑4↓) or stepwise (2↓3↑).
rules: Major only (in minor the segment ②–⑥ fails on the diminished triad; in major ③–⑦ fails).
guidelines: ♭3 on ⑤ optional to announce the minor quality of ii and vi.
Canonic version with (8–)4–3 for practical composition.
2½ segments + comma (regular comma or Corelli long comma).
3 segments: deviation back to the main key (5♯ on ⑦), or the third segment rises a third (④–①).
Can be tonicized (upper, lower or both voices).

sources.notes: Moti del Basso pp.31–32; HCP Notes p.11

checks: HCP Terms: bass a fifth up and a fourth down; 4–3 suspension on second chord; segments ③–⑦ (major) and ②–⑥ (minor) omitted; canonic variant.
Demeyere: 2, 2½, 3 segments; Corelli long comma; regular comma; tonicization; major only.

patterns.name: Quiescenza
function: proposta (1st half 18th c., once, unequal stages)
closing (2nd half 18th c., twice in a row, after a clausula basizans)
patterns.summary: Tonic pedal with 4–5 sonorities: 5/3 – (7♭/5/3) – 6/4 – 7♮/4/2 – 8/5/3. The temporary departure (d5→3, toward IV) and return (A4→6) strengthen the tonic.
rules: Chromatic element: lowered ⑦ in major; raised ③ in minor; raised ④ on a ⑤ pedal (both modes).
guidelines: Often announced by a trill on ②.
Minor proposta: the augmented second ⑥–⑦♯ can be avoided (Bach BWV 999 turns ⑤–⑥–④–③), borrowed (⑥♯), or kept (Cimarosa).
Insert 6/4/2 between 6/4 and 7♮/4/2 (Do-Ti-Te-La-Ti-Do counterpoint).
Hermaphrodite Quiescenza: ⑥♭ in major — darker.
Quiescenza-Ponte: ⑤–④–③–④♯–⑤ over a ⑤ pedal, prolongs a half cadence and bridges back (K.550/i, bars 38–42).

sources.notes: Moti del Basso pp.33–34; HCP Notes p.10

checks: HCP Terms: pedal on ① or ⑤; d5→3 and A4→6; chromatic element ♭7 (major), ♯3 (minor), ♯4 on ⑤.
Demeyere: Gjerdingen’s 4–5 sonorities; proposta (Bach) vs closing (Cimarosa, Mozart); BWV 999 and Cimarosa C36 minor solutions; trill on ➋.

patterns.name: Ponte
patterns.summary: Dominant pedal with parallel thirds or sixths and no fixed structure; rhetorically effective right after ‖: .
guidelines: Melodic-minor inflections (②♯, ③♯) in the rising line.

checks: HCP preface: Riepel coined Fonte and Monte; “Another term, the Ponte, does not occur in HCP.”
flags: No Ponte page on essaysonmusic.com; verify against Gjerdingen if needed.

patterns.name: Indugio
patterns.melody: ② (with lower neighbour ①♯), often ②–④–⑥ ascent at the end
patterns.summary: Lingers on ④ to increase the expectation of closure; typically ends with the converging cadence (④–♯④–⑤) and its high ⑥ drop.
guidelines: Bass ④ can be embellished by the lower neighbour ③; treble ② by ①♯.
②–④–⑥ ascent = temporary focus on the ii key; perfect for connecting to the high ⑥ drop.
With 5/3 triad (V7/IV, vii°/IV → IV) = temporary focus on the ④ key.
With N6 (②♭): popular in minor, possible in major (temporary minor).

variants.name: Circular Indugio
variants.description: Three-part, most common: bass ④–⑤–⑥–⑤–④, treble ②–③–④–③–② in parallel sixths, pedal ① in the middle voice; 6/5 – passing 6/4 – 6/3; usually repeated twice.

variants.name: Chromatic circular Indugio
variants.description: ♯④ starts each rotation (V6/5/V → I6/4); add the melodic inversion for 4 parts.

variants.name: With (6–)7–6 suspension
variants.description: Upper voice holds over the barline (Mozart K.279).

variants.name: Cadenza finta (feigned cadence)
variants.description: Pedals on ① and ③; or the interrupted circular Indugio (bass leaps ③→④), or set as a deceptive cadence (Valente).

variants.name: Metrically shifted circular Indugio
variants.description: Bass ⑥–⑤–④–⑤–⑥ with ⑥ strongest; 6/3 – passing 6/4 – 6/5.

checks: Demeyere: pedal on ④ with 6 or 6/5; converging cadence; triad start; Neapolitan sixth; circular Indugio rotations, cadenza finta (Valente), interrupted, metrically shifted.

patterns.name: Fenaroli
patterns.bass: ① ② ③ ⑦ | ① ② ③ ⑦ | ① (circling the tonic)
patterns.melody: ⑦–① … ②–③ (imitating the bass) over a ⑤ pedal in another voice
patterns.summary: Three components: bass circling ①; one upper voice imitating the bass (canonic); another holding ⑤. Usually repeated twice.
rules: Harmonies follow the RO, except 6/4 on ②.
guidelines: All sorts of diminutions may obscure it.

sources.notes: Moti del Basso p.39; HCP Notes p.12

checks: HCP Terms: three components; RO except 6/4 on ②.

patterns.name: Romanesca + Prinner
patterns.bass: ① ⑦ | ⑥ ③ | ④ ③ ② ⑤ | ①
patterns.summary: Romanesca (gambit) answered by a Prinner (riposte) at twice the harmonic rhythm; often followed by a modulating Prinner.
guidelines: Other combinations to explore: Prinner + Fonte/Meyer; Monte + Fonte; Fonte + Monte.

checks: Demeyere page exists: “Combinations of a Romanesca and a Prinner”.
